I am happy to announce that I have formalized a proof of the famous result in distributed computing about the impossibility of distributed consensus with even one faulty process due to Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson:
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3149.214121
My code can be found at:
https://github.com/ctchou/cslib/tree/flp-work/Cslib/Computability/Distributed/FLP
The proof I formalized is not the original one in the FLP paper, but the one by Völzer:
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0020019004001887
Völzer's proof was previously formalized in Isabelle/HOL:
https://www.isa-afp.org/entries/FLP.html
But my Lean proof is done independently from scratch with a rather different formalization and seems much shorter than the Isabelle/HOL proof (1067 lines vs 4521 lines). To be sure, my proof doesn't have comments yet, but adding comments will probably increase the code size by only 10% or so.

In the following weeks I will add comments, clean up the code, and split it into multiple PRs for cslib.
Congratulations, @Ching-Tsun Chou!! Looking forward to the PRs! :⁠-⁠)

I took a look at the Isabelle/HOL formalization of Völzer's proof and tried to figure out why that proof is so much longer than mine. I can discern several possible causes:
(1) I can rely on a lot of definitions and results already in mathlib (mainly List and Multiset) and cslib (mainly ωSequence and LTS). I estimate that developing that necessary background theory "cost" the Isabelle/HOL proof at least 1000 lines of code. Except for one small result (cslib#532), I didn't need to prove any such results.
(2) For reasons I don't understand, the Isabelle/HOL proof chose to model an infinite sequence as a map from ℕ to increasing finite prefixes of the infinite sequence. Consequently the definition of an execution being fair looks like this:

Here's the equivalent definition in the Lean proof:

def ProcFair (p : P) (ss : ωSequence (State P M S)) (xs : ωSequence (Action P M)) : Prop :=
  ∀ m, m.dest = p → ∀ k, m ∈ (ss k).msgs → ∃ j, k ≤ j ∧ xs j = some m

Perhaps this difference in modeling infinite sequences has some implication on proof lengths.
(3) I borrowed Leslie Lamport's idea of always allowing a stuttering step in system execution. This enables me to not worry about what happens when a system runs out of messages to receive. (Fairness constraints like the one above can exclude pathological executions in which a message is ready to be received but is never received.). This trick may have helped to reduce code size, but I'm not sure.
(4) There is one result in Völzer's paper which the author considered so obvious that he didn't bother to supply even an informal argument:

Perhaps I was missing something, but I found it actually one of the hardest proofs in the entire formalization. Fortunately, I was able to find a common machinery that can be used in proving both this result and the main result of the paper (Theorem 1).

Could you help me understand your proof please? It is quite long. Concretely could you point me to your definition of bivalent executions, indistinguishable executions, and where you show that a bivalent execution (or its equivalent) can be forcibly extended to another? I guess I am missing some docstrings that would point me in the right direction.

I'll look forward to reviewing! Please do consider what can be extracted for separate PRs. We don't have a formal template or CI like Mathlib for it, but dependent PRs are welcome.

On the docs note, it'd probably be overkill for this amount of code, but I do look forward to hopefully having contributions that follow the pattern of having a blueprint. Great for both the author and reviewer to have this sort of overview to follow where the docs are written along the way.

Don't worry. I will add comments and doc strings, though probably not in the next few days as I feel a bit exhausted now. I'll probably PR each file separately.

Before I add the comments, please note that other than the technical results in FairScheduler.lean, my code actually follows Völzer's paper quite closely and the technical contents of that paper are only 3.5 pages long. Völzer does not use the notion of "bivalency" as in the original FLP paper, but uses the notion of "non-uniformity" instead. I'm actually not aware of any complete formalization of the original FLP paper.

I actually tried to experiment with vibe coding (when I first learnt to use agents) by getting an agent to formalise the version of FLT my advisor teaches in his course. I can try to finish it if you will find it useful for your PRs. I ensured that the basic definitions are fairly clean, so it is not entirely slop.

I guess you meant FLP, not FLT?

The definitions and theorems in my files Algorithm.lean and Consensus.lean are not specific to Völzer’s approach and may be useful to you. The final result (the last theorem in Impossibility.lean) is stated in terms of those definitions alone.

That's so bizarre I felt compelled to double check, and wow, yeah, correctInfinite (via infiniteExecution) really does imply a single ℕ-indexed sequence o_O
Maybe they designed it with CTL in mind?

Sorry, I neglected to mention where I took the scrrenshot from. It was this paper:
https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-43144-4_7
So far as I can tell, there is no temporal logic in the Isabelle/HOL formalization.

Looking at that paper again, I'm not sure that the Isabelle/HOL proof actually formalized the notion of a (fault-tolerant) consensus algorithm. Yes, they formalized the notion of a (fault-tolerant) pseudo-consensus algorithm, which is a key idea in Völzer's proof. But the ultimate goal is to prove the non-existence of any consensus algorithm, not that of pseudo-consensus algorithm. (Indeed, Völzer wouldn't have written the sentence I quoted above if he only cared about pseudo-consensus algorithms.) I did a cursory search in the Isabelle code and could not find a definition of a consensus algorithm.

I have added comments to all Lean files and added a README:
https://github.com/ctchou/cslib/tree/flp-work/Cslib/Computability/Distributed/FLP
I have also opened the first PR: cslib#556

I opened a new PR cslib#619 which presents a simple distributed consensus algorithm and proves that it achieves consensus if there is no fault. This result is not needed for proving the FLP impossibility result, but is included to show that the notion of an algorithm defined in Algorithm.lean is not vacuous, in the sense that it does allow a working consensus algorithm when there is no fault.
It would be great if someone can review my PRs cslib#612 and cslib#619. Thanks in advance!
